issues.legal_issue: A compulsory-acquisition law that fixes compensation by reference to an unrelated earlier valuation date, without relevant circumstances justifying that date, does not provide compensation as required by the applicable legislative limitation.
material_facts: Land was compulsorily acquired for a housing scheme after a notification under the general acquisition law.

The amending law required compensation to be based on the land's value on a fixed date earlier than the acquisition notification, whichever valuation was lower, and removed the additional amount otherwise payable for compulsory acquisition.
The earlier date had no relevant connection to the acquisition or to circumstances requiring the value to be assessed at that time.
issues.conclusion: The amending law did not provide compensation that was the just equivalent of what the owner was deprived of and was void for contravening the legislative limitation on compulsory acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, and held that its compensation requirement was pari materia with Article 31(2) of the Constitution as it stood before amendment. Following State of West Bengal v. Mrs. Bela Banerjee, compensation must be a just equivalent of the property taken; whether the stated principles account for relevant elements of value is justiciable. A fixed anterior valuation date without relevant justification is arbitrary. The rule does not differ merely because the law is temporary rather than permanent.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_chal: The case challenges a law governing compensation for compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.compensation_uses_unrelated_earlier_valu: The law bases compensation on a valuation date earlier than the acquisition notification, without tying that date to the acquisition process.
predicates.no_relevant_reason_for_earlier_date: No relevant circumstance requires the property's value to be assessed on the earlier date.

issues.definition: When a compulsory-acquisition compensation challenge involves an unrelated earlier valuation date with no relevant justification, the acquisition law is invalid for inadequate compensation.

issues.legal_issue: A law that was void for want of legislative competence when enacted cannot qualify as an existing law protected from constitutional challenge.
material_facts: The challenged acquisition law was enacted before the Constitution commenced.
The law did not satisfy the compensation condition that limited the legislature's power to authorize compulsory acquisition.
The law was not certified under the constitutional procedure that could protect certain pre-commencement laws despite non-compliance with that condition.
issues.conclusion: The law was void from its inception and was not an existing law protected by Article 31(5)(a).
issues.legal_principle: Under section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, providing for compensation was a condition on legislative power, and a law made without satisfying that condition was a nullity. Article 366(10) defines an existing law as one made by a legislature or other body having power to make it. Articles 31(5) and 31(6), read together, do not save a law that was void when made; unlike clause (5), clause (6) expressly provides a route for certification of certain laws that did not comply with section 299(2). The court referred to H. P. Khandalwal v. State of U.P., Assistant Collector, Thana Prant v. Jamnadas Gokuldas Patel, and State of West Bengal v. Bon Behari Mondal.

predicates.pre_constitution_acquisition_law_challen: The case challenges a law concerning compulsory acquisition that was enacted before the Constitution commenced.
predicates.law_lacked_power_condition_when_enacted: The legislature enacted the law without satisfying a condition on its power to authorize compulsory acquisition.
predicates.no_constitutional_certification: The law did not receive the certification available under the constitutional procedure for certain pre-commencement laws.

issues.definition: If a pre-commencement acquisition law was enacted without a condition on legislative power and received no applicable certification, it is not saved as an existing law.

issues.legal_issue: Constitutional protection for laws concerning acquisition of estates does not revive a pre-constitutional law that was void from its inception.
material_facts: The challenged law was void from its inception because it failed to satisfy the pre-constitutional condition on legislative power.
The law therefore had no legal existence when the Constitution commenced.
The State relied on the constitutional protection for laws concerning acquisition of estates or rights in estates.
issues.conclusion: Article 31-A did not save the law because it had no legal existence when the Constitution commenced.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31-A protects laws within its scope from specified challenges based on rights under Articles 14, 19 and 31, but does not revive laws that were void when enacted. The court distinguished Dhiruba Devisingh Gohil v. State of Bombay and State of U.P. v. H. H. Maharaja Brijendra Singh, which concerned the distinct protection in Article 31-B. Article 31-B is not governed by Article 31-A and is not merely illustrative of laws that would otherwise fall within Article 31-A.

predicates.pre_constitution_acquisition_law_challen: The case challenges a law concerning compulsory acquisition that was enacted before the Constitution commenced.
predicates.law_was_void_when_enacted: The law was void at the time it was enacted because the legislature lacked power to enact it in that form.
predicates.law_had_no_legal_existence_at_constituti: The law had no legal existence when the Constitution commenced.

issues.definition: A pre-commencement acquisition law that was void when enacted and had no legal existence at commencement is not revived by protection for laws concerning estates.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional protection for statutes specifically listed in the constitutional schedule operates independently of the protection for laws concerning acquisition of estates.
material_facts: The State relied on decisions concerning laws included in the constitutional schedule to argue that constitutional protection for scheduled laws supported its interpretation of the separate protection for estate-acquisition laws.

The court held that the provision protecting scheduled laws gives those specified statutes protection from attacks based on Part III even when they do not fall within the separate estate-acquisition protection.
issues.conclusion: Article 31-B is an independent constitutional device that protects the specified statutes from attacks on the ground that they infringe Part III; it is not governed by Article 31-A or merely illustrative of its scope.
issues.legal_principle: The court construed Articles 31-A and 31-B together, relying on Article 31-B's express protection for the statutes specified in the Ninth Schedule, including protection notwithstanding court judgments. The words 'without prejudice to the generality' indicate that the specified statutes may have immunity even if they do not attract Article 31-A. The court distinguished Dhiruba Devisingh Gohil v. State of Bombay and State of U.P. v. H. H. Maharaja Brijendra Singh on this basis.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: The case challenges a statute on the ground that it violates constitutional rights in Part III.
predicates.statute_is_specifically_listed_in_consti: The statute challenged is one specifically listed in the constitutional schedule that provides it protection.

issues.definition: In a constitutional validity challenge, a statute specifically listed in the constitutional schedule is immune from a Part III challenge independently of the separate estate-acquisition protection.
